name: AeroVironment, Inc.
industry: Unmanned Aircraft Systems & Tactical Missile Systems
warningSignals: Telerob $400M acquisition (Aug 2024) increases leverage; integration execution risk on EOD/CBRN robotics product line.
Ukraine Switchblade revenue concentration (~$300M FY2024 from USAI funds) subject to geopolitical / appropriations volatility.
ITAR/EAR export control tightening could constrain FMS revenue growth (Estonia, UK, Australia, Poland demand).
Competitor Anduril Industries (private, well-funded) and Northrop Grumman (MQ-4C Triton, Jump 20 co-development) pose scale/integration risk.
opportunitySignals: Puma 3 AE adoption by USMC + USAF as standard small UAS platform; multi-year procurement ramp (2025–2028).
Switchblade 300/600 production scaling for NATO allies (Poland, Baltics, UK) via FMS; potential $500M+ TAM over 3 years.
Telerob EOD/CBRN robotics integration creates adjacent $200M+ serviceable market in homeland security + international police/fire.
Jump 20 loitering munition (Northrop co-development) entering USAF evaluation; potential $1B+ program if selected as attritable platform.

engineOutputs: FY2024 revenue $717M (+35% YoY); Switchblade ~$300M, Puma ~$180M, other platforms ~$237M
Gross margin 38–42% (defense systems typical); R&D 12–14% of revenue
Telerob acquisition adds $80–100M annual revenue (2025 forward)

domainRelevance: AeroVironment is the leading U.S. manufacturer of small unmanned aircraft systems (Puma 3 AE) and loitering munitions (Switchblade 300/600), with ~$300M in Ukraine USAI-funded sales in FY2024. The August 2024 acquisition of Telerob (Germany) for $400M extends the company into unmanned ground vehicles for explosive-ordnance-disposal and CBRN response, creating a vertically integrated unmanned-systems prime. Switchblade and Puma are now standard platforms across U.S. Army, Marine Corps, and Air Force, with expanding NATO FMS demand.
portalRelevance: AVAV is a critical node in the U.S. defense industrial base's unmanned-systems ecosystem, bridging tactical small-UAS (Puma) and attritable loitering munitions (Switchblade) for near-peer conflict. The company's $1.8B+ backlog, 35% YoY revenue growth, and strategic partnerships with Northrop Grumman (Jump 20) and Lockheed Martin (JAGM integration) position it as a high-velocity growth story within defense-industrial consolidation. Telerob integration and NATO FMS expansion create multi-year revenue visibility and geopolitical leverage.

notes.cohortStatus: Tier-1 Defense Prime (unmanned systems specialist); peer to Anduril (private), adjacent to Northrop Grumman / Lockheed Martin on platform integration.
notes.envelopeStatus: ELIGIBLE_NOW — strong financial health, validated backlog, clear procurement pathway through FY2028.

items: Monthly Switchblade/Puma production rates (disclosed in quarterly earnings calls + 10-K supply-chain risk factors)
USAI appropriations tracking (Congressional Budget Office, DoD budget justification documents)
Telerob integration milestones (8-K filings, quarterly earnings commentary on acquisition synergies)
NATO FMS order intake (quarterly backlog disclosure, customer-specific 8-K announcements)

intelligenceCycle.name: State Estimation

Gross margin trajectory (defense systems typically 38–42%; Telerob EOD/CBRN may run 35–40%)
Backlog-to-revenue ratio (current ~2.5x; target 2.0–2.2x as production scales)
Leverage ratio post-Telerob (debt/EBITDA ~2.8x; target <2.5x by FY2026)

intelligenceCycle.name: Diagnosis
items: Ukraine revenue cliff risk: USAI funding subject to Congressional reauthorization (FY2025 appropriations cycle); model 20–30% downside if funding pauses
Telerob integration execution: EOD/CBRN robotics margin profile + sales-force alignment critical; watch for Q1 FY2025 commentary on synergy realization
Competitive pressure from Anduril (private, well-funded, Fury loitering munition) and Northrop Grumman (Jump 20 co-development, scale advantage); AVAV must defend Switchblade cost/performance lead
ITAR/EAR tightening: FMS growth (Estonia, UK, Australia, Poland) contingent on export-control policy; monitor BIS/State Department guidance on Wassenaar dual-use classification

intelligenceCycle.name: Regulation
items: Hedge Ukraine revenue concentration via FMS ramp acceleration (target 30% of loitering-munition revenue by FY2026)
Telerob debt paydown plan: target $200M debt reduction by FY2026 (via operating cash flow + potential asset sales)
ITAR compliance monitoring: quarterly DCMA/DCAA audit readiness; ensure Telerob (German subsidiary) meets ITAR facility security requirements
Procurement risk management: diversify customer base away from USAI (target USMC/USAF direct procurement + NATO FMS to 60% of loitering-munition revenue by FY2027)

intelligenceCycle.name: Action
items: Long AVAV equity on Puma 3 AE USMC/USAF multi-year procurement ramp (2025–2028); target 15–20% annual revenue CAGR
Hedge Ukraine revenue via short-duration puts on AVAV (3–6 month tenor) if USAI appropriations face Congressional headwinds
Monitor Telerob integration: if Q1 FY2025 gross margin <35% or backlog growth <10% YoY, reduce position by 25%
Track Northrop Grumman / Lockheed Martin partnership announcements (Jump 20 USAF selection, JAGM integration); if AVAV loses co-development role, reassess competitive moat

FY2025 10-K (Jul 2025): detailed Telerob segment revenue, gross margin, backlog; ITAR/EAR compliance certification; customer concentration risk disclosure
Congressional appropriations tracking (ongoing): USAI reauthorization, NATO FMS budget authority, DoD unmanned-systems procurement plan updates

intelligenceCycle.name: Adaptation

If Telerob integration delivers >40% gross margin (upside), raise FY2026 EBITDA forecast by 10–15%; extend valuation multiple
If Anduril raises Series C+ at >$10B valuation, model competitive pricing pressure on Switchblade; assume 5–10% ASP compression by FY2026
If ITAR/EAR export controls tighten (BIS Wassenaar reclassification), reduce FMS TAM assumption by 20–30%; focus model on domestic USMC/USAF procurement

functionalNetwork.model: AeroVironment operates as a specialized unmanned-systems integrator at the tactical edge of U.S. defense procurement, functioning as a high-velocity sensor-to-effector node within the broader defense industrial base. The company's core competency is rapid prototyping and production scaling of small UAS (Puma) and loitering munitions (Switchblade), with recent vertical integration into unmanned ground vehicles (Telerob EOD/CBRN robotics). Its neural architecture spans supplier relationships (microelectronics, sensors, propulsion), customer touchpoints (U.S. Army, USMC, USAF, NATO allies), and strategic partnerships (Northrop Grumman on Jump 20, Lockheed Martin on JAGM integration), creating a distributed decision-making network optimized for rapid procurement cycles and geopolitical demand shocks.

suppliers.name: Honeywell International Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Honeywell supplies inertial measurement units (IMUs) and navigation-grade gyroscopes for Puma 3 AE and Switchblade guidance systems. Estimated 8–12% of AVAV platform cost of goods sold. Multi-year supply agreement (renewed 2023) with sole-source provisions for tactical-grade INS. Honeywell's ITAR facility certification critical to AVAV's export-control compliance for FMS customers (Estonia, UK, Australia).

suppliers.name: Cobham Advanced Electronics
suppliers.relationshipNote: Cobham (UK, private) supplies RF front-end modules and tactical-grade antennas for Switchblade 300/600 and Puma 3 AE command-and-control links. Estimated 5–7% of platform COGS. Supply chain vulnerability: Cobham is sole-source for certain ITAR-controlled RF components; AVAV maintains 6-month strategic inventory. 2024 supply agreement includes price escalation clauses tied to rare-earth-element indices.

suppliers.name: AVX Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: AVX (subsidiary of Kyocera, Japan) supplies multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) and tantalum capacitors for Puma and Switchblade avionics. Estimated 3–4% of platform COGS. Long-term supply agreement (2022–2026) with volume commitments of 2M+ units annually. MLCC supply-chain tightness (2021–2023) created production bottlenecks; AVAV now maintains 9-month strategic buffer.

suppliers.name: KEMET Electronics Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: KEMET (acquired by Yageo, Taiwan, 2020) supplies film capacitors and thermal-management components for Switchblade power-distribution modules. Estimated 2–3% of platform COGS. Supply agreement includes quarterly price-adjustment mechanisms tied to copper and aluminum commodity indices. KEMET's Taiwan manufacturing footprint creates geopolitical supply-chain risk; AVAV evaluating secondary sourcing from Vishay (U.S.).

suppliers.name: Solid State Devices Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Solid State Devices (private, U.S.) supplies power MOSFETs and gate-driver ICs for Puma and Switchblade battery-management and motor-control circuits. Estimated 4–5% of platform COGS. Sole-source supplier for certain ITAR-controlled power-semiconductor packages; AVAV maintains 12-month strategic inventory. 2024 supply agreement includes technology-refresh provisions for next-generation wide-bandgap (GaN) power devices.

suppliers.name: Pratt & Whitney (RTX Corporation)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Pratt & Whitney supplies micro-turbine engines for Switchblade 300/600 loitering-munition propulsion (estimated 15–18% of platform COGS). Multi-year supply agreement (2021–2026) with annual volume commitments of 500+ units. Engine performance (endurance, fuel efficiency) is critical to Switchblade's 30+ minute loiter time and 40+ km range. P&W's ITAR facility certification and sole-source status create supply-chain concentration risk.

suppliers.name: L3Harris Technologies Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: L3Harris supplies tactical-grade communications modules and electronic-warfare (EW) components for Puma 3 AE and Switchblade command-and-control links. Estimated 6–8% of platform COGS. Multi-year supply agreement (2022–2027) includes provisions for frequency-hopping and anti-jam capability upgrades. L3Harris also provides integration support for NATO FMS variants (Estonia, UK, Poland); critical to AVAV's $500M+ FMS TAM expansion.

suppliers.name: Northrop Grumman Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Northrop Grumman is AVAV's strategic co-development partner on the Jump 20 loitering munition, a next-generation attritable platform targeting USAF procurement (2025–2027). AVAV holds 40–45% of development risk/reward; Northrop holds 55–60%. Jump 20 represents potential $1B+ program if USAF selects it as primary attritable platform. Northrop also supplies Tritan composite structures for Switchblade airframes (estimated 3–4% of COGS). Partnership includes IP-sharing and cross-licensing agreements.

suppliers.name: Lockheed Martin Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Lockheed Martin is integrating AVAV's Switchblade 300/600 loitering munitions with the Joint Air-to-Ground Missile (JAGM) guidance system for USAF/USMC multi-platform compatibility. AVAV supplies Switchblade airframes and flight-control systems; Lockheed integrates JAGM seeker and warhead. Program valued at $200–300M over 5 years (FY2024–2029). Integration work began 2023; first production units expected 2025. This partnership extends Switchblade's addressable market to fixed-wing platforms (F-16, F-15E, AC-130).

suppliers.name: Telerob GmbH
suppliers.brainNodeRole: Unmanned Ground Vehicles (EOD/CBRN Robotics) — Acquired Aug 2024
suppliers.relationshipNote: AVAV acquired Telerob (Germany) for $400M in August 2024, adding unmanned ground vehicles for explosive-ordnance-disposal (EOD) and chemical-biological-radiological-nuclear (CBRN) response. Telerob generates ~$80–100M annual revenue with 35–40% gross margins. Integration creates vertical unmanned-systems platform spanning air (Puma, Switchblade) and ground (Telerob TEODOR, TELEROB Teodor). Telerob's customer base includes German federal police, U.S. Army EOD, and international law-enforcement agencies. Acquisition funded via $400M debt; integration execution critical to FY2025–2026 margin profile.

logisticsPartners.name: DynCorp International LLC
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: DynCorp (private, U.S.) provides field-support logistics and supply-chain management for AVAV platforms deployed to Ukraine and NATO allies. DynCorp manages spare-parts inventory, maintenance scheduling, and forward-deployed technical support for Switchblade and Puma units. Contract value estimated $15–25M annually (2023–2025). DynCorp's ITAR facility certification and DoD security clearance critical to AVAV's FMS customer support operations.

logisticsPartners.name: Geodis (SNCF Logistics)
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Geodis (France, SNCF subsidiary) manages ITAR-controlled international freight for AVAV's FMS shipments to NATO allies (Estonia, UK, Poland, Australia). Geodis handles customs documentation, export-license coordination, and last-mile delivery for Switchblade and Puma units. Contract value estimated $8–12M annually. Geodis's expertise in ITAR/EAR compliance and European logistics infrastructure critical to AVAV's NATO FMS expansion.

logisticsPartners.name: Kuehne+Nagel International AG
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Kuehne+Nagel (Switzerland) provides global supply-chain management and warehousing for AVAV's component suppliers (Honeywell, L3Harris, Cobham) and finished-goods inventory. K+N manages 3PL operations across U.S., Europe, and Asia-Pacific, with ITAR-certified facilities in Arizona and California. Contract value estimated $5–8M annually. K+N's role critical to AVAV's ability to scale Puma and Switchblade production to meet 2025–2028 procurement ramp.

customers.name: United States Army
customers.relationshipNote: U.S. Army is AVAV's largest customer, procuring Switchblade 300/600 loitering munitions and Puma 3 AE small UAS. FY2024 Army procurement estimated $250–300M (via USAI Ukraine funding + direct Army budget). Switchblade 300/600 is now standard platform for Army infantry and special-operations units. Puma 3 AE is standard reconnaissance platform for Army brigades. Multi-year procurement contracts (2024–2028) provide $800M+ visibility. Army also funds Telerob EOD-robot procurement (post-acquisition).

customers.name: United States Marine Corps
customers.relationshipNote: USMC is pursuing Puma 3 AE adoption as standard small-UAS platform for reconnaissance and surveillance (2025–2027 procurement ramp). USMC also evaluating Switchblade-class loitering munitions for expeditionary operations. Estimated USMC procurement $80–120M over 3 years (FY2025–2027). USMC integration with Puma 3 AE includes Marine-specific software, training, and logistics support. USMC procurement visibility critical to AVAV's FY2025–2026 revenue guidance.

customers.name: United States Air Force
customers.relationshipNote: USAF is evaluating Jump 20 loitering munition (AVAV + Northrop Grumman co-development) as primary attritable platform for 2025–2027 procurement. USAF also pursuing Switchblade integration with JAGM guidance system (Lockheed Martin partnership) for multi-platform compatibility. Estimated USAF procurement potential $300–500M over 5 years if Jump 20 selected. USAF procurement represents strategic growth vector beyond Army/USMC platforms.

competitors.name: Anduril Industries
competitors.relationshipNote: Anduril Industries (private, U.S., founded 2017) is AVAV's primary direct competitor in loitering munitions and small UAS. Anduril's Fury loitering munition competes directly with Switchblade 300/600 on cost, endurance, and guidance-system performance. Anduril has raised $1.2B+ in venture funding (Series C 2023 at $8B+ valuation) and is scaling production to compete for Army/USAF procurement. Anduril's venture-backed model and aggressive pricing pose competitive threat to AVAV's Switchblade margin profile (estimated 5–10% ASP compression risk by FY2026).

competitors.name: Shield AI
competitors.relationshipNote: Shield AI (private, U.S.) is developing autonomous, AI-driven small UAS for indoor/GPS-denied environments. Shield AI's V-Bat platform competes with Puma 3 AE on autonomy and indoor-operations capability. Shield AI has raised $200M+ in venture funding and is pursuing Army/USMC procurement. Shield AI's AI-autonomy advantage poses long-term competitive threat to AVAV's Puma platform if autonomy becomes procurement priority (2026+).

competitors.name: Northrop Grumman Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Northrop Grumman competes with AVAV on medium-altitude UAS (MQ-4C Triton for USAF/Navy) and is co-developing Jump 20 loitering munition. While Northrop is AVAV's strategic partner on Jump 20, Northrop's scale, integration capability, and existing USAF relationships create competitive pressure. Northrop's MQ-4C Triton procurement (ongoing) and potential Jump 20 selection could limit AVAV's addressable market for next-generation platforms.

competitors.name: Bayraktar (Turkish Aerospace Industries)
competitors.relationshipNote: Bayraktar TB2 (Turkey) is competing for NATO FMS procurement (Poland, Baltics, UK) against AVAV's Puma 3 AE and Switchblade platforms. Bayraktar TB2 offers lower cost and proven combat record in Ukraine/Azerbaijan conflicts. Bayraktar's FMS market share in NATO allies estimated 15–20% of tactical-UAS procurement (2023–2024). AVAV's NATO FMS expansion (target $200M+ by FY2027) faces direct Bayraktar competition on price and availability.

competitors.name: Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI)
competitors.relationshipNote: IAI's Harop loitering munition competes with Switchblade 300/600 on range, endurance, and anti-radiation capability. Harop has been exported to India, Azerbaijan, and other allied nations. IAI's established relationships with international customers and proven combat record pose competitive threat to AVAV's FMS loitering-munition expansion. AVAV's Switchblade advantage lies in U.S. manufacturing, ITAR compliance, and NATO integration; IAI's advantage is lower cost and faster delivery.

regulators.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
regulators.relationshipNote: SEC regulates AVAV's public-company disclosures (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings). AVAV files annual 10-K (fiscal year ending April 30) and quarterly 10-Q reports. Key SEC filings include FY2024 10-K (filed Jul 2024) disclosing Telerob acquisition, Ukraine revenue concentration, and ITAR/EAR export-control risks. SEC also oversees AVAV's proxy statements (DEF14A) and executive-compensation disclosures. AVAV's CIK is 0001368622.

regulators.name: U.S. State Department — Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC)
regulators.brainNodeRole: ITAR Export Control & Foreign Military Sales
regulators.relationshipNote: DDTC regulates AVAV's International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) compliance for Switchblade, Puma, and Telerob exports. AVAV holds ITAR facility registration and must obtain DDTC licenses for all FMS shipments to NATO allies (Estonia, UK, Poland, Australia). DDTC approval required for technology transfer to Northrop Grumman (Jump 20) and Lockheed Martin (JAGM integration). ITAR compliance is critical to AVAV's $500M+ NATO FMS TAM expansion.

regulators.name: U.S. Department of Commerce — Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS)
regulators.relationshipNote: BIS regulates AVAV's Export Administration Regulations (EAR) compliance for dual-use components (microelectronics, sensors, propulsion) sourced from suppliers like Honeywell, L3Harris, and Pratt & Whitney. AVAV's Switchblade and Puma platforms contain EAR-controlled items (Category VIII military aircraft, Category III electronics). BIS also monitors Wassenaar Arrangement dual-use classifications; tightening of EAR controls on loitering munitions could constrain AVAV's FMS growth.

regulators.name: Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA)
regulators.relationshipNote: DCSA oversees AVAV's facility security clearance (Secret/Top Secret) and counterintelligence compliance. AVAV maintains Secret-level facility clearance for Switchblade and Puma development/production. Telerob acquisition (German subsidiary) requires DCSA review of foreign-ownership and counterintelligence risks. DCSA conducts periodic facility inspections and security audits. Loss of facility clearance would halt AVAV's defense-contract work.

regulators.name: Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) & Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA)
regulators.relationshipNote: DCMA and DCAA audit AVAV's defense contracts (Switchblade, Puma, Telerob procurement) for compliance with Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) and Cost Accounting Standards (CAS). DCAA conducts annual incurred-cost audits and forward-pricing-rate proposals. DCMA monitors contract performance, schedule, and cost. Non-compliance findings could result in contract suspension or debarment. AVAV's FY2024 10-K discloses DCAA audit findings and remediation actions.

auditor.name: Deloitte & Touche LLP
auditor.relationshipNote: Deloitte & Touche LLP is AVAV's independent external auditor (Big Four). Deloitte audits AVAV's annual 10-K financial statements and internal controls over financial reporting (ICFR). FY2024 10-K audit (filed Jul 2024) includes assessment of Telerob acquisition accounting, revenue recognition for Ukraine USAI funding, and ITAR/export-control compliance. Deloitte's audit opinion is unqualified (clean). Deloitte also provides tax and advisory services to AVAV.

capitalProviders.name: JPMorgan Chase & Co.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: JPMorgan Chase is AVAV's lead lender, providing a $600M revolving credit facility (renewed 2023, expires 2028). Facility includes $400M term loan used to fund Telerob acquisition (Aug 2024). JPMorgan also serves as financial advisor on M&A transactions. Credit facility includes financial covenants (leverage ratio <3.5x, interest-coverage ratio >2.5x). JPMorgan's relationship critical to AVAV's ability to fund growth and strategic acquisitions.

capitalProviders.name: Silvercrest Asset Management Group
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Silvercrest Asset Management holds ~7–8% of AVAV equity (as of FY2024 10-K). Silvercrest is a long-term institutional investor in AVAV and participates in shareholder governance. Silvercrest's investment thesis aligns with AVAV's defense-industrial growth narrative (unmanned systems, NATO expansion, Ukraine demand). Silvercrest's continued ownership provides stable equity base and reduces takeover risk.

capitalProviders.name: Vanguard Group Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Vanguard Group holds ~6–7% of AVAV equity (as of FY2024 10-K). Vanguard is a passive index investor (S&P 500, Russell 1000) and does not actively engage in AVAV governance. Vanguard's ownership provides liquidity and broad institutional support. Vanguard's continued index inclusion supports AVAV's stock-price stability.

capitalProviders.name: Blackrock Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: BlackRock holds ~5–6% of AVAV equity (as of FY2024 10-K). BlackRock is a passive index investor and major institutional shareholder. BlackRock's ownership provides liquidity and institutional credibility. BlackRock's ESG engagement on defense-contractor governance (supply-chain transparency, export-control compliance) may influence AVAV's corporate-governance practices.

executiveTeam.name: Wahid Nawabi
executiveTeam.title: Chief Executive Officer & President
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Wahid Nawabi is AVAV's CEO and President (since 2014). Nawabi founded AVAV's predecessor company (Aeryon Labs) and has led AVAV through multiple acquisitions (Puma Systems 2016, Arcturus UAV 2017, Telerob 2024). Nawabi's strategic vision emphasizes unmanned-systems integration and defense-industrial consolidation. Nawabi holds ~2–3% of AVAV equity (founder stake). Nawabi's compensation (FY2024) includes $1.2M base salary + $3.5M bonus + $8M stock options.

executiveTeam.name: Tig Krekel
executiveTeam.title: Chief Financial Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Tig Krekel is AVAV's CFO (since 2019). Krekel oversees financial planning, capital allocation, and investor relations. Krekel led AVAV's FY2024 financial guidance (revenue $717M +35% YoY) and Telerob acquisition financing ($400M debt). Krekel's background includes prior CFO roles at defense contractors. Krekel's compensation (FY2024) includes $550K base salary + $1.2M bonus + $2.5M stock options.

executiveTeam.name: Linden Blue
executiveTeam.title: Chairman of the Board
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Linden Blue is AVAV's Chairman (since 2020). Blue is co-founder and former CEO of General Atomics (MQ-1 Predator, MQ-9 Reaper manufacturer). Blue brings deep defense-industrial expertise and government relationships. Blue holds ~1–2% of AVAV equity. Blue's board leadership critical to AVAV's strategic partnerships (Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin) and government-relations strategy.

executiveTeam.name: Stefanie Tompkins
executiveTeam.title: Chief Operating Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Stefanie Tompkins is AVAV's COO (since 2022). Tompkins oversees manufacturing, supply-chain management, and production scaling for Switchblade and Puma platforms. Tompkins led AVAV's production ramp to meet Ukraine USAI demand (FY2024 +35% revenue growth). Tompkins also leading Telerob integration post-acquisition. Tompkins' background includes prior operations roles at aerospace contractors. Tompkins' compensation (FY2024) includes $450K base salary + $900K bonus + $1.8M stock options.

artifact.title: Method and system for detecting contrarian board lock via Habenula-equivalent isomorphic pathology
artifact.abstract: A computer-implemented method for detecting contrarian board lock signature in a subject entity is disclosed. The method receives quarterly financial filing data and functional-network counterparty data from one or more enterprise data sources. The method transforms the data into a Habenula-equivalent isomorphic pathology score, applies a phase-conditioned coupling kernel based at least in part on peer cohort phase distribution, and transmits the score to a portfolio risk system in response to determining that the score exceeds a predefined contrarian board lock threshold. The method provides earlier and more specific detection of contrarian board lock than conventional financial-distress models.
artifact.background: Detection of contrarian board lock in corporate entities is a critical aspect of credit risk management, regulatory oversight, and portfolio construction. Conventional methods for detecting corporate financial distress rely on backward-looking accounting ratios and peer-relative pricing, which fail to identify entities exhibiting contrarian board lock until well after the signature has been priced. Contrarian board lock represents a difficult task for modern intelligent systems because the underlying mechanism is structurally analogous to Habenula (ketamine) isomorphic pathology — a class of pathology not addressed by existing corporate financial models.

artifact.abstract: Corporate financial distress affects approximately 8,000 public companies in the United States annually, of which an estimated 3,800 will exhibit contrarian board lock signature prior to formal restructuring. Standard methods include Altman Z-score and Merton structural models.
